summary: The note examines third-party risk management (TPRM) in the financial sector, prompted by a September 15, 2023 cyber-attack on a major payment processor. It covers regulatory updates from the FFIEC and EBA, frameworks like ISO 27001 and the SIG questionnaire, due diligence, continuous monitoring, contracts, cyber insurance, AI, and employee training. It concludes that institutions need adaptive, collaborative TPRM programs with tested incident response plans.
one_line: Financial institutions must strengthen third-party risk management through regulation, due diligence, monitoring, contracts, insurance, technology, and training after a 2023 payment processor attack.
key_facts: On September 15, 2023, a cyber-attack on a major payment processor exposed vulnerabilities that third-party providers introduce to financial institutions.
Janae Thompson, head of cybersecurity at Finastra Bank, said third-party breaches can have a cascading effect on multiple connected entities.

On October 1, 2023, the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (FFIEC) in the United States issued revised TPRM guidelines stressing thorough due diligence and continual monitoring of all third-party providers.
On November 20, 2023, the European Banking Authority (EBA) released revised regulatory technical standards on third-party risk, mandating a more proactive and comprehensive approach to TPRM.
ISO 27001 provides a blueprint for establishing, implementing, and maintaining an information security management system (ISMS).
The Shared Assessments Program's Standardized Information Gathering (SIG) questionnaire can streamline risk assessments by creating consistent evaluation criteria.
Andrew Li, a cybersecurity analyst, said "due diligence is the first line of defense against third-party cyber risk."
Continuous monitoring, for example via security ratings services, gives institutions realtime insight into vendors' security posture.
Vendor contracts should spell out cybersecurity requirements, incident response obligations, and liability clauses, according to the note and Matthew Harper of FinSecure Consulting.
Cybersecurity insurance can cover legal fees, regulatory fines, and compensation for lost business, but Dr. Erin Patel says it is not a replacement for robust cybersecurity controls.
Rajeev Singh, CEO of SecureFinTech, said advanced tech such as AI and machine learning can enhance detection of and response to third-party risks.
Anne-Marie Walters, a cybersecurity trainer, stressed that every employee plays a crucial role in the organization's cybersecurity posture.

The note calls for tested incident response plans that incorporate third-party vendors, and for collaboration and threat intelligence sharing among regulators, institutions, vendors, and professionals.
